bp: The ordinary-world problem is a workplace trying to understand what its people are actually doing with AI assistants. The evidence is not a clean survey form. It is many back-and-forth conversations: a worker asks for help, clarifies, corrects the assistant, changes direction, and eventually reaches some work product or abandons the attempt. Leaders, product designers, and researchers may want to know which kinds of work these assistants support, where they seem useful, and what designs should improve next. Reading conversations one by one does not scale, but treating them as raw text piles misses the shape of the work. This paper serves that gap. HILTON is built to turn multi-turn assistant conversations into a topic map: first shorter descriptions of what each conversation was about, then groups of similar conversations, then higher-level topic structure, with humans correcting the map so it remains practically meaningful rather than merely machine-made.
wh: The hard part is that a conversation is not a single clean document. It contains several turns, repeated wording, failed attempts, side questions, and context that may only become clear after the last message. If a system groups conversations by surface words alone, two sessions about the same workplace task may look different because one user says "draft this note" and another says "make this sound professional." The reverse can also happen: two conversations may share words but serve different purposes. A fully manual taxonomy has the opposite problem. Humans can judge whether a topic makes sense, but they cannot cheaply read and organize every new conversation as usage grows. The abstract also emphasizes new data arriving over time, so the topic map cannot be frozen. It must discover new patterns, keep old useful categories, and remain understandable to people who will use the analysis for design or assessment.
naive: A smart beginner might export all conversations, count common words, and make a chart of frequent terms. A slightly stronger version would run an automatic grouping method directly on the raw conversation text and name each group by its most common words. This fails because frequent words are often not the same as work intent. Long conversations include greetings, corrections, copied documents, assistant phrasing, and repeated instructions. Those details can drown out the real task. Another beginner might ask human annotators to label every conversation, but that becomes slow and expensive as new assistant logs arrive. The paper's starting point is therefore a tradeoff: automatic discovery is scalable but noisy, while human judgment is meaningful but scarce.
ap: The paper's central move is to separate the job into stages that match the strengths of machines and people. First, a large language model is used as a summarizer: it compresses a multi-turn conversation into a shorter statement of what happened. This gives the later grouping step cleaner material than the raw transcript. Second, the summaries are grouped without requiring a fixed list of topics in advance. The abstract calls this unsupervised, non-parametric clustering; in plain terms, the system looks for natural piles in the data and is not forced to decide beforehand that there must be exactly ten or twenty topics. Third, those groups are organized into a hierarchy, so narrow topics can sit under broader ones. Finally, human annotators edit and judge the discovered groups. Their feedback refines the topic structure and creates evaluation data for later rounds.
mech: The mechanism begins with a stream or collection of workplace conversations between users and AI assistants. Each conversation has several turns, so the first transformation is summarization. A language model reads the full exchange and produces a compact description of the conversation's main purpose. That summary is still text, but it is less cluttered than the original interaction. Next, the system compares summaries and places similar ones into clusters, meaning groups whose members appear to describe related work. Because the clustering is described as non-parametric, the pipeline is meant to allow the number and shape of topics to emerge from the data rather than from a fixed hand-written list. The discovered clusters are then arranged hierarchically: small, specific topic groups can be collected under broader categories, giving analysts both close detail and a higher-level overview. As new conversations arrive, the structure can be dynamically updated instead of rebuilt as a one-time report. Human annotators then inspect the machine-discovered clusters, adjust topic labels or boundaries, and provide feedback. That corrected output becomes a cleaner topic map and also becomes evaluation data. The final stage trains a lightweight statistical classifier, a cheaper prediction model, so unseen conversations can be assigned to topics efficiently without rerunning the whole human-review process every time.
math: The mathematics is about compression, similarity, grouping, hierarchy, and learning from corrected examples. Summarization is compression with judgment: many turns are squeezed into fewer words, and the system must keep the purpose of the exchange while dropping repetition and noise. Clustering is grouping by measured resemblance. The system needs some way to decide that two summaries are close enough in meaning to belong together, even if they do not use identical wording. Non-parametric clustering means the method is not locked to a preselected number of groups; this fits workplace assistant use because organizations may not know the task categories before looking. Hierarchy adds a tree-like structure: a broad topic can contain smaller subtopics, so the same data can be read at different levels of detail. Human feedback turns the problem into supervised learning for later use. Once annotators correct clusters and labels, the lightweight classifier learns a rule from examples: when a new conversation summary has certain signs, assign it to a likely topic. The key tradeoff is discovery versus control. Open-ended grouping finds unexpected uses, while human correction prevents mathematically tidy but practically useless topics from becoming the final map.
dots: This paper sits at the intersection of topic modeling, language-model applications, and human-centered data mining. Like other text mining papers, it tries to turn messy language into organized evidence. Like clustering work, it asks how to sort a large pile when there is no trusted label for every item. Like efficiency papers, it separates an expensive high-quality process from a cheaper deployment step: deep summarization, clustering, and human correction create the topic structure, while the lightweight classifier makes everyday inference fast. It also connects to the broader conference interest in AI assistants and agents, but from the measurement side rather than the assistant-behavior side. The sibling idea is evaluation and analytics for LLM use: before improving an assistant, defending it, or personalizing it, a workplace must first know what tasks people are bringing to it and which topic boundaries make sense to humans.
ww: The method should work better than raw clustering because it changes the object being grouped. A raw transcript contains the user's task, the assistant's responses, repairs, boilerplate, and sometimes pasted material. A summary aims to keep the task-level meaning while removing details that would mislead a grouping method. That gives similarity measurement a cleaner target: conversations are compared by what they were trying to accomplish, not merely by repeated words. The human loop helps for a different reason. Topic quality is partly a social and organizational judgment. A cluster can be statistically coherent and still be useless if it joins tasks that workplace analysts need to separate, or splits tasks that they view as one category. Annotator feedback supplies that missing judgment and turns it into data for future refinement. The lightweight classifier works because, after the expensive discovery and correction stages have created examples, many future conversations can be handled as a faster recognition problem rather than a full discovery problem.
po: The payoff is a practical pipeline for workplace analytics of AI assistant use. The abstract claims HILTON produces coherent topic structures for multi-turn assistant conversations, supports hierarchical organization, updates as new data arrives, and includes human feedback to improve quality and practical relevance. It also produces evaluation data for future iterations and trains a lightweight statistical classifier for efficient topic inference on unseen conversations. That buys two capabilities at once: open-ended discovery of what people use assistants for, and cheaper repeated categorization once the topic map has been refined. The open-source code further makes the approach reusable beyond the authors' own application.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The summaries must preserve the real work intent of the conversations; if the summarizer drops a key turn or overstates what happened, every later stage inherits that error. The clustering must find groups that correspond to meaningful workplace tasks, not just patterns in phrasing. Human annotators must understand the domain well enough to correct clusters consistently, and their feedback may reflect local business priorities rather than universal topic boundaries. Dynamic updates can also disturb old categories if new data changes the structure. The abstract reports coherent topic structures, but it does not give the exact datasets, annotation rules, classifier accuracy, privacy handling, or evidence that the topics remain stable across different organizations.
